analytical_question: Can both shifts operate a four-week shadow pilot now, and can the retailer sustain routine use?
general_et_finding: An item tag can identify an individual garment during a count; the GS1 case establishes deployment precedent, not local accuracy.
application_finding: Comparing a shadow count of denim with manual recounts can expose stock discrepancies. A tag read alone cannot establish which stock record needs correction.
organization_specific_finding: Sponsorship supported: four-week sponsor commitment. Skills supported for counting: two leads passed exercise. Workflow gap: the drill logged a mismatch but no one accepted or escalated it. Infrastructure/data supported for scope: reader, verified tag mapping and barcode fallback. Resources mixed: pilot funded; operating budget ends at week four. Governance supported for corrections: controller approval and no scan writeback. Culture/change partially supported: one reported mismatch without penalty, too little to infer store-wide trust. Operating ownership gap: a signed roster names cover, but the observed drill contradicts effective coverage.

evidence.claim: I.T.’S. international used individually tagged garments for inventory counts in apparel stores.
evidence.date_or_recency: GS1 Japan case study, 2012; reviewed November 8, 2026.
evidence.notes: Establishes precedent; no transfer of time savings or present staffing readiness.

evidence.claim: Sponsor funds four weeks of one-store shadow counts. Two shift leads passed a count exercise; staff logged a mismatch without penalty. Stockroom has a reader, verified tag-to-SKU list and barcode recount procedure. Inventory Controller approves ledger corrections after recount; scans cannot write to the ledger. One named floor lead plus a trained deputy can collect counts. Both shifts have reserved count time. A signed roster gives the closing lead and deputy queue coverage, recount time and escalation to the controller before any correction. In the completed drill the deputy logged the mismatch; nobody accepted or escalated it by shift close. The ledger stayed unchanged. No ongoing budget beyond week four.
evidence.notes: Accepted for the exercise; not audited employer records.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: Roster and training support preparation. The synthetic drill is stronger evidence about actual handoff behavior; one failed drill does not show RFID failed.
confidence_and_uncertainty: High confidence in the scoped judgment given the case facts; actual execution is unverified.
value_opportunity_implication: Count fully reconciled size/color discrepancies and total staff time, including exception work. Fast scanning alone cannot show operational value.
risk_governance_implication: Keep scans read-only. Escalate unresolved records rather than silently adjusting stock; controller retains correction authority.
recommendation_management_implication: Hold the two-shift pilot. Keep manual counts authoritative. Have store operations agree who acknowledges the queue and by when; repeat the closing drill with the controller unavailable. Require recorded acceptance or escalation before authorizing both shifts. Daytime read-only practice tests scanning only.
change_monitoring_triggers: Repeat the failed handoff. A signed roster alone does not reverse the hold.

Proposed week-four rule: sponsor may consider routine use only with a complete exception log, every discrepancy accepted by a named owner or explicitly escalated by shift close, no overdue unresolved cases, zero unauthorized ledger corrections, and a funded roster whose reserved hours cover measured work. Missing logs: withhold. A missed handoff: hold, repair and retest. An unauthorized correction: stop immediately and investigate.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: Routine use is not ready. Ask the sponsor for a recurring budget and signed staffing plan.
